body:
The legal foundation of chemical emergency planning

India has specific rules for preventing and preparing for major chemical accidents. The Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules, 1989 address obligations associated with hazardous chemicals and major-accident-hazard installations. The Chemical Accidents (Emergency Planning, Preparedness and Response) Rules, 1996 establish crisis-management arrangements for chemical accidents.

Both sets of rules operate within the broader framework of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. They complement the all-hazard disaster-management institutions rather than replacing them.

On-site and off-site emergency plans

The most important distinction is whether planning concerns consequences within the industrial site or consequences that may extend beyond its boundary.

PlanMain area of concernPrimary responsibility
On-site emergency planEmergency arrangements within the industrial installationOccupier or operator of the covered hazardous installation
Off-site emergency planConsequences affecting people and areas outside the installationCompetent authority, involving factory-inspection and district authorities

Under Rule 13 of the 1989 Rules, the occupier is responsible for the on-site emergency plan where the relevant requirements apply. Under Rule 14, off-site emergency planning is the responsibility of the designated competent authority. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change has explained the off-site arrangement in terms of the Chief Inspector of Factories working in consultation with district authorities.

The off-site plan must take account of information supplied by the industrial installation. This linkage matters because the district cannot plan meaningful public warnings or protective arrangements without knowing the general nature of relevant hazards and the potentially affected area.

On-site: the industrial occupier prepares for an emergency at the installation. Off-site: the competent public authority plans for consequences beyond the installation boundary. The plans must be coordinated.

Crisis groups under the 1996 Rules

The 1996 Rules establish specialised crisis groups at different levels for chemical-accident preparedness and response.

GroupLevelMain role
Central Crisis GroupNationalNational guidance and coordination on major chemical accidents
State Crisis GroupStateState-level coordination and review of district off-site plans
District Crisis GroupDistrictSupport district off-site planning, review on-site plans and coordinate chemical-accident preparedness
Local Crisis GroupIndustrial pocketLink local planning with the district plan and educate potentially affected communities

The District Crisis Group is the apex district body under these rules for dealing with major chemical accidents. Under Schedule 7, it is chaired by the District Collector, and the Inspector of Factories serves as Member-Secretary.

Its duties under Rule 9 include assisting with the district off-site plan, reviewing relevant on-site plans, supporting the district administration during chemical accidents and maintaining communication with state and central crisis-management arrangements. Rule 9 requires the District Crisis Group to conduct at least 1 full-scale chemical-accident mock drill at a site each year.

The Local Crisis Group operates at the industrial-pocket level. Under Rule 10, it prepares a local emergency plan, connects that plan with the district off-site plan and helps educate nearby populations about possible chemical accidents and appropriate preparedness.

District Crisis Group and DDMA are not the same body

The District Crisis Group is a specialised institution created under the 1996 chemical-accident rules. The District Disaster Management Authority is an all-hazard district institution under the Disaster Management Act, 2005. Their functions can overlap in practice, and the Collector has an important role in both, but the bodies have different legal foundations and responsibilities.

Warning the community during a chemical accident

An effective public warning should identify the danger, the area potentially affected, the protective action to take and the source of further authoritative information. Sirens, official mobile messages, public-address systems, local administration, police and other recognised channels may be used according to local arrangements.

The correct immediate public action depends on the chemical and incident. Shelter-in-place may be instructed when remaining inside a suitable building offers better immediate protection from an outdoor airborne release. Residents may then be told to close doors and windows and stop ventilation that draws outside air indoors. Evacuation may instead be directed when leaving by a specified safe route is safer. Neither response should be treated as a universal rule for every chemical release.

People should avoid approaching the incident, touching unknown substances, entering contaminated areas or relying on rumours. A cloth over the mouth is not reliable protection against hazardous gases. Residents should follow the latest instructions from competent authorities and seek medical attention if exposure is suspected or symptoms develop.

Post-accident recovery and public safety

After the immediate emergency, recovery includes medical support, assessment of affected areas, restoration of safe drinking water and public services, and communication about safe return. Environmental contamination may require assessment before restrictions on access or use are lifted.

As of the content cutoff of 2 November 2026, GSDMA's public website lists a State Crisis Plan (Chemical Disaster Management Plan) 2026. This is a dated state planning document; the legal distinctions explained above are based on the cited national rules.

One integrated view of Gujarat's major hazards

Effective preparedness connects each hazard with the most suitable technical warning, protective action and responsible institution. Cyclone and flood management often focuses on advance weather information, inundation risk and safe movement. Drought management focuses on sustained water and livelihood security. Heat management focuses on public-health protection. Chemical-disaster management depends particularly on facility information, off-site planning and incident-specific community instructions.

Prelims focus

  • Environment (Protection) Act: 1986.
  • Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules: 1989.
  • Chemical Accidents (Emergency Planning, Preparedness and Response) Rules: 1996.
  • Rule 13 concerns on-site emergency plans; Rule 14 concerns off-site emergency plans.
  • The District Crisis Group is chaired by the District Collector, with the Inspector of Factories as Member-Secretary.
  • Trap: The District Crisis Group under the 1996 Rules and the DDMA under the 2005 Act are distinct institutions. Likewise, shelter-in-place and evacuation are alternative protective responses, not simultaneous instructions for every chemical incident.

[Sources: Government of India, Environment (Protection) Act, 1986; Manufacture, Storage and Import of Hazardous Chemicals Rules, 1989, Rules 13 and 14; Ministry of Environment and Forests, Chemical Accidents (Emergency Planning, Preparedness and Response) Rules, 1996, Rules 3–10 and Schedules 5–8, Gazette notification G.S.R. 347(E), 1 August 1996; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, notice F. No. 14-6/2016-HSMD, 8 August 2016, paragraphs 1–3; Disaster Management Act, 2005, district authority provisions; GSDMA, State Crisis Plan (Chemical Disaster Management Plan) 2026, listing checked 2 November 2026.]
